# OneCoin / “Cryptoqueen” Fraud Scheme: Evidence-Bounded Reconstruction

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence describes OneCoin as an international cryptocurrency investment fraud that began operating in Bulgaria in 2014 and was based in Sofia. The U.S. Department of Justice identifies Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood as co-founders who, together with others, orchestrated the scheme between 2014 and 2019. OneCoin marketed and sold a cryptocurrency of the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. According to the returned enforcement account, victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The available evidence supports a broad operating model: members purchased OneCoin packages, recruited additional purchasers, and received commissions connected to those recruitments. The government’s allegations, as summarized by ArentFox Schiff, were that OneCoin’s purported value was arbitrarily set rather than determined by supply and demand, and that no publicly verifiable blockchain actually existed despite representations that one did. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

Greenwood is documented as having been sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. Ignatova is identified as a co-founder, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive, and a person who remains at large. The returned evidence does not establish her whereabouts, whether she is alive or dead, or any specific account involving a yacht, murder, body recovery, or forensic identification. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The evidence also documents a DOJ remission process announced on April 13, 2026. More than $40 million in forfeited assets was stated to be available for victim compensation. The returned sources do not identify all prosecuted participants or provide source-supported roles or case outcomes for Konstantin Ignatov, Mark Scott, Irina Dilkinska, or other individuals beyond Greenwood and Ignatova.

## Scope and evidentiary limits

This report is limited to the two source records returned by the benchmark tools:

- **SRC-001:** a U.S. Department of Justice announcement concerning compensation for OneCoin victims.
- **SRC-002:** an ArentFox Schiff summary of Greenwood’s sentencing and the government’s account of the scheme.

The benchmark searches sought additional material concerning OneCoin’s chronology, recruitment structure, other defendants, and Ignatova’s possible whereabouts or death, including searches directed at the FBI, BBC, Guardian, Financial Times, and additional DOJ material. No additional source IDs or excerpts were returned. Those unreturned materials therefore cannot be used as evidence here.

The following distinctions are important:

- **Established enforcement or procedural facts:** facts expressly reported by the DOJ or by the sentencing summary, such as Greenwood’s sentence and the existence of a remission process.
- **Government allegations or prosecutorial accounts:** descriptions of how OneCoin allegedly operated, including the alleged absence of a public blockchain and arbitrary valuation.
- **Law-enforcement characterizations:** statements by DOJ, FBI, IRS-CI, or U.S. Attorney officials describing the conduct and its effects.
- **Unresolved matters:** issues not established by the returned source excerpts, including Ignatova’s current location, survival, or death.

## Origins and chronology

### Formation and Bulgarian base

The DOJ states that OneCoin began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. ArentFox Schiff similarly reports that OneCoin began operating in Bulgaria in 2014. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The DOJ identifies Ignatova and Greenwood as co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. and states that they, together with others, orchestrated the international investment scheme between 2014 and 2019. This is an enforcement characterization of their alleged leadership and conduct. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

### United States operations

The ArentFox Schiff summary states that OneCoin began operating in the United States around 2015. The returned DOJ excerpt does not provide additional detail about the U.S. launch, its personnel, or its regional structure. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Enforcement-period chronology

The evidence supports the following limited chronology:

| Date or period | Supported event | Evidentiary classification |
|---|---|---|
| 2014 | OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria and was based in Sofia. | Reported by the DOJ and secondary legal source. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison) |
| 2014–2019 | Ignatova, Greenwood, and others are described by the DOJ as having orchestrated the international investment scheme. | DOJ enforcement characterization. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) |
| Around 2015 | OneCoin began operating in the United States. | Reported in the secondary legal summary. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison) |
| June 2022 | Ignatova was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List. | Reported enforcement/status fact. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison) |
| September 15, 2023 | ArentFox Schiff published its account of Greenwood’s sentence. | Publication and reported sentencing date. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison) |
| April 13, 2026 | DOJ announced a remission process for OneCoin victims. | DOJ procedural announcement. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) |
| October 1, 2026 | Research cutoff. The returned evidence still provides no confirmed location, death, or survival finding for Ignatova. | Evidence-bounded conclusion; not an independently established real-world status update. |

The evidence does not establish a more detailed chronology of OneCoin’s creation, expansion, internal restructuring, or collapse.

## Operating model

### Cryptocurrency marketing

The DOJ describes OneCoin as a fraudulent cryptocurrency marketed and sold through a global MLM network. The product was sold under the OneCoin name, and victims purchased it during the period covered by the enforcement account. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The evidence supports describing OneCoin as an investment product presented to purchasers as cryptocurrency. It does not establish, from the returned excerpts alone, every technical feature of the purported token, the precise software architecture, or the complete process by which purchasers allegedly acquired, held, or exchanged it.

### Alleged valuation mechanism

According to the government’s account summarized by ArentFox Schiff:

- OneCoin’s value was represented as being determined by market supply and demand.
- The government alleged that its value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces.
- Greenwood allegedly represented that OneCoin had a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions.
- The government alleged that no public, verifiable blockchain actually existed. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

These are allegations or prosecutorial assertions as reported by a secondary legal source. The returned excerpts do not provide an independent technical audit, blockchain analysis, or separate adjudicated finding explaining the precise technical condition of OneCoin’s systems.

### Financial scale

The DOJ states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide as a result of misrepresentations about OneCoin. ArentFox Schiff likewise describes the matter as a $4 billion fraud scheme and reports that the government charged Greenwood and others with obtaining more than $4 billion in investments from approximately 3.5 million investors. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The figures should be read with their different evidentiary bases:

- **More than $4 billion:** reported by the DOJ as the amount invested by victims worldwide.
- **Approximately 3.5 million investors:** reported only in the ArentFox Schiff summary of the government’s case.
- The DOJ excerpt does not independently repeat the 3.5 million figure.

The DOJ describes the losses as “monumental” and states that victims were misled by falsified statements and empty promises, causing them to deplete savings in an investment system that would not pay out. Those descriptions are law-enforcement characterizations quoted in the DOJ announcement. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

## Recruitment, MLM, and marketing structure

### Global MLM network

Both returned sources describe OneCoin as using a global multi-level-marketing structure. The organization therefore did not rely solely on direct sales by a central company; it used members to market the product to additional purchasers. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The evidence specifically supports this simplified model:

1. OneCoin offered cryptocurrency packages.
2. Existing members recruited additional people to purchase packages.
3. Members received commissions associated with recruitment-linked purchases.
4. The network operated internationally.
5. Greenwood was described as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Greenwood’s alleged distributor income

ArentFox Schiff reports the government’s allegation that Greenwood earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, amounting to more than $300 million, in his role as the top MLM distributor. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The returned evidence does not provide:

- Payment records supporting the calculation.
- A complete description of the commission formula.
- The identity of all distributors.
- The number or names of distributor levels.
- Specific package prices.
- Recruitment quotas or sales targets.
- Regional management structures.
- Conference, event, or advertising details.
- The percentage of sales retained by the central organization versus affiliates.

Accordingly, the 5% and $300 million figures should be presented as government allegations reported in the secondary source, not as independently verified financial findings in the benchmark evidence.

## Principal founders and documented roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The evidence supports the following limited description of Ignatova:

- She was identified by the DOJ as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd.
- She was described, together with Greenwood and others, as having orchestrated the scheme between 2014 and 2019.
- She was identified as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive.
- ArentFox Schiff reported that she was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022.
- She remained at large according to the returned source material. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

Her role as co-founder is directly stated by both sources. Her alleged role in orchestrating the fraud is an enforcement characterization. The evidence does not provide a separately supported description of her precise operational responsibilities, such as product development, finance, recruiting, regional control, or specific transactions.

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

The evidence supports the following description of Greenwood:

- He was a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd.
- He was described by the DOJ as having orchestrated the scheme with Ignatova and others.
- He was described by ArentFox Schiff as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor.
- He was alleged to have earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling more than $300 million.
- He was sentenced to 20 years in prison.
- He was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

The sentence and forfeiture are reported as completed judicial outcomes by the secondary source. The returned excerpt does not specify the precise conviction counts, statutory provisions, verdict date, sentencing judge, or the calculation underlying the forfeiture amount.

### Other individuals

The DOJ refers to Ignatova and Greenwood acting “and others.” It also states that several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced. However, the returned excerpts do not name those other figures or document their roles, charges, pleas, convictions, or sentences. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

In particular, the benchmark evidence does not support a factual account of the roles or outcomes of:

- Konstantin Ignatov;
- Mark Scott;
- Irina Dilkinska; or
- any other participant not expressly described in SRC-001 or SRC-002.

Their names were among the subjects sought in the research queries, but search intent is not evidence and cannot establish a role or case result.

## Enforcement actions and judicial outcomes

### Greenwood’s sentence

ArentFox Schiff reports that Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in the $4 billion fraud scheme and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

This is the clearest individual judicial outcome in the returned material. The source title describes Greenwood as a co-founder of the fraudulent cryptocurrency, while the excerpt frames some underlying conduct as government allegations. The available evidence does not permit a more specific account of the conviction counts or sentencing rationale.

### Broader prosecutions

The DOJ states that it filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York and that several key figures had been sentenced. It also states that the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the fraud scheme. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The returned evidence does not identify all prosecutions, defendants, charges, plea agreements, verdicts, or sentences. It therefore supports only the general conclusion that the OneCoin matter generated multiple U.S. prosecutions and more than one sentence.

### Investigative agencies

The DOJ states that the FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation and that the DOJ’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

These are documented agency roles in the returned DOJ account. The evidence does not provide a complete description of the investigation’s international partners, investigative methods, or evidentiary record.

## Victim compensation and forfeiture

### Remission process

On April 13, 2026, the DOJ announced the beginning of a remission compensation process for victims of the OneCoin investment scheme. The DOJ stated that more than $40 million in forfeited assets was then available for victim compensation. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The process is managed by the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, with Kroll Settlement Administration LLC serving as remission administrator. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The announcement states that people who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible. It identifies a June 30 filing deadline, although the returned excerpt does not make clear which year applies to that deadline. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

### Application information

The DOJ announcement states that victims could obtain a petition form through the OneCoin remission website or request one from the remission administrator by telephone, email, or mail. It also states that the DOJ and remission administrator would not charge victims to participate. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

The returned evidence gives the following contact information:

- Website: `www.onecoinremission.com`
- Telephone: `1-833-421-9748`

The broader DOJ statement that its Asset Forfeiture Program had returned more than $12.5 billion to crime victims since 2000 concerns the program generally and should not be treated as a OneCoin-specific recovery figure. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

## Ruja Ignatova’s whereabouts, status, and possible death

### What is established in the returned evidence

The sources support the following statements:

- Ignatova is identified as a co-founder of OneCoin.
- She is described as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive.
- She was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022, according to SRC-002.
- She remains at large, according to SRC-002.
- The FBI continued pursuing her and sought information about her, according to SRC-001. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

These facts establish an enforcement status—not a verified physical location or proof of life.

### What remains unresolved

The returned evidence does not establish:

- Ignatova’s current location;
- whether she is alive;
- whether she is dead;
- a date or place of death;
- a yacht-related killing;
- a murder order;
- the identity of a suspected killer;
- recovery of remains;
- forensic identification; or
- a confirmed investigative conclusion that she died.

The searches sought accounts concerning her disappearance and possible death, but no additional source IDs or source excerpts were returned. Therefore, those accounts cannot be treated as benchmark-supported findings.

As of the requested October 1, 2026 cutoff, the most precise evidence-bounded conclusion is that Ignatova’s status is unresolved beyond the fact that the returned enforcement sources describe her as wanted and at large. “At large” should not be converted into a conclusive claim that she is alive, just as the absence of a confirmed arrest should not be converted into a claim that she died.

## Differences between the returned sources

No direct contradiction is apparent between SRC-001 and SRC-002 on the core account. Both sources:

- place OneCoin’s origins in Bulgaria in 2014;
- describe it as a fraudulent cryptocurrency sold through an MLM network;
- identify Ignatova and Greenwood as co-founders;
- report losses of approximately or more than $4 billion; and
- describe Ignatova as absent from custody and sought by authorities.

There are differences in scope and detail:

### Investor count

SRC-002 reports approximately 3.5 million investors as part of the government’s case. SRC-001 reports more than $4 billion invested worldwide but does not state an investor count. This is an omission or difference in detail, not a contradiction. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Greenwood’s alleged earnings

SRC-002 reports the allegation that Greenwood received 5% of monthly sales and earned more than $300 million. SRC-001 does not provide those figures. The difference reflects source coverage, not conflicting accounts. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Forfeiture amounts

SRC-002 attributes approximately $300,000 in forfeiture to Greenwood. SRC-001 states that more than $40 million in forfeited assets was available for victim compensation. The figures concern different scopes: one is attributed to Greenwood, while the other concerns the broader pool available for remission. They do not directly conflict. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

### Chronology

SRC-001 describes the relevant scheme period as 2014–2019. SRC-002 adds that OneCoin began operating in the United States around 2015. The latter is a geographic detail within the broader period and does not conflict with the DOJ chronology. [SRC-001](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered) [SRC-002](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

## Consolidated conclusions

The benchmark evidence supports the following conclusions:

1. OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and was based in Sofia.
2. It was marketed as a cryptocurrency investment and sold through a global MLM network.
3. Members were described as receiving commissions for recruiting people who purchased cryptocurrency packages.
4. The DOJ attributes more than $4 billion in worldwide victim investment to misrepresentations about OneCoin.
5. The government alleged that OneCoin’s value was arbitrarily set and that no publicly verifiable blockchain existed, despite representations concerning a blockchain.
6. Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood are identified as co-founders.
7. Ignatova is described as a co-founder and wanted fugitive who remains at large in the returned evidence.
8. Greenwood is documented as having been sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture.
9. The DOJ states that multiple OneCoin prosecutions occurred and that several key figures were sentenced, but the returned excerpts do not identify all of them.
10. A DOJ remission process began in April 2026, with more than $40 million in forfeited assets stated to be available for victim compensation.
11. The returned evidence does not establish Ignatova’s location, survival, death, or any specific death-related account.
12. No source-supported role or case outcome should be assigned here to other named individuals not described in the returned excerpts.
